source_text: Πῶς οὖν ἄτοπον ἐπὶ μὲν τῶν βιωτικῶν πραγμάτων πρὸ τῶν φανερῶν τὰ ἀφανῆ βλέπειν, καὶ πρὸ τῶν μισθῶν ὑπομένειν τοὺς πόνους, καὶ πρότερον τὰ δυσχερῆ πάντα φέροντας, τότε τὰ ἐξ αὐτῶν ἀναμένειν χρηστὰ, καὶ ταῖς τῶν ἀφανῶν ἐλπίσι προτρεπομένους οὕτως ἅπτεσθαι τῶν φανερῶν· ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ Θεοῦ διστάζειν καὶ ἀμφιβάλλειν, καὶ πρὸ τῶν πόνων ἀπαιτεῖν τὰς ἀμοιβὰς, καὶ γεωργῶν καὶ ναυτῶν μικροψυχοτέρους φαίνεσθαι; Οὐ γὰρ δὴ μόνον κατὰ τοῦτο αὐτῶν φανούμεθα χείρους, ἀσχάλλοντες πρὸς τὸ μέλλον, ἀλλὰ καὶ καθ' ἕτερον οὐκ ἔλαττον τούτου. Ποῖον δὴ τοῦτο; Ὅτι ἐκεῖνοι μὲν οὐδὲ περὶ τοῦ τέλους θαῤῥεῖν ἔχοντες πάντως, οὐδὲ οὕτω τῶν πόνων ἀφίστανται· σὺ δὲ ἀξιόπιστον τῶν στεφάνων ἔχων ἐγγυητὴν, οὐδὲ οὕτω μιμῇ τὴν ἐκείνων καρτερίαν. Ὁ μὲν γὰρ γεωργὸς πολλάκις μετὰ τὸ τὰ σπέρματα καταβαλεῖν, καὶ θεραπεῦσαι τὴν γῆν, καὶ κομῶντα τὰ λήϊα ἰδεῖν, ἢ χαλάζης, ἢ ἐρυσίβης, ἢ ἀκρίδος. ἢ ἄλλης τινὸς τοιαύτης ἐπενεχθείσης πληγῆς, ἐξέπεσε τῆς τῶν πόνων ἀμοιβῆς, καὶ μετὰ τοὺς πολλοὺς ἱδρῶτας κεναῖς οἴκαδε ὑποστρέφει χερσί. Καὶ ὁ ἔμπορος δὲ πάλιν, μετὰ τὸ διαδραμεῖν πολὺ πέλαγος πεπληρωμένην ἄγων τὴν ὁλκάδα, πρὸς αὐτὸ πολλάκις τὸ στόμα τοῦ λιμένος ἐμπεσόντων ἀνέμων σκοπέλῳ τινὶ προσαράξας, μόλις ἐξῆλθε τὸ σῶμα διασώσας γυμνός. Καὶ ἐπὶ πάντων ἁπλῶς τῶν βιωτικῶν πολλὰς πολλάκις πρὸς τῷ τέλει συμφορὰς τοιαύτας συμβαίνειν εἰκός. Ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ἀγώνων τῶν σῶν οὐκ ἔστι τοῦτο· ἀλλὰ ἀνάγκη πάντως τὸν ἀγωνισάμενον, τὸν σπείραντα τὴν εὐσέβειαν, καὶ πολλοὺς ἐνεγκόντα πόνους, ἐπιτυχεῖν τοῦ τέλους. Οὐ γὰρ ἀέρων ἀνωμαλίαις, οὐδὲ πνευμάτων ῥύμαις τῶν πόνων τούτων τὰς ἀμοιβὰς ἐπέτρεψεν ὁ Θεός· ἀλλ' ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς ἀπόκεινται, ἐν τοῖς ἀσύλοις θησαυροῖς. Διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ὁ Παῦλος ἔλεγεν· Ἡ θλῖψις ὑπομονὴν κατεργάζεται, ἡ δὲ ὑπομονὴ δοκιμὴν, ἡ δὲ δοκιμὴ ἐλπίδα, ἡ δὲ ἐλπὶς οὐ καταισχύνει. Μὴ τοίνυν εἴπῃς ὅτι ἀφανῆ τὰ μέλλοντα· εἰ γὰρ βουληθείης μετὰ ἀκριβείας ἐξετάσαι, τῶν ἐν χερσίν ἐστι πολὺ φανερώτερα. Καὶ τοῦτο αὐτὸ πάλιν ἐνδεικνύμενος ἡμῖν ὁ Παῦλος, Τὰ μὲν αἰώνια καλεῖ, τὰ δὲ πρόσκαιρα, τῷ προσκαίρῳ τὸ φθαρτὸν αὐτῶν δηλῶν. Πρὶν ἢ γὰρ φανῆναι ἀφίπταται, καὶ ἀποτρέχει πρὶν ἐπιστῆναι, καὶ ὀξύῤῥοποι μὲν αὐτῶν αἱ μεταβολαὶ, ἄπιστος δὲ ἡ κτῆσις. Τοῦτο καὶ ἐπὶ πλούτου καὶ δόξης καὶ δυναστείας, καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς τῶν σωμάτων εὐμορφίας, τοῦτο καὶ ἐπὶ ῥώμης καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἁπλῶς τῶν βιωτικῶν συμβαῖνον ἴδοι τις ἄν. Διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ὁ προφήτης κωμωδῶν τοὺς τρυφῶντας καὶ περὶ χρήματα μαινομένους καὶ τὴν ἄλλην ἅπασαν φαντασίαν, Ὡς ἑστῶτα, φησὶν, ἐλογίσαντο ταῦτα, καὶ οὐχ ὡς φεύγοντα. Ὥσπερ γὰρ σκιᾶς οὐκ ἔστιν ἐπιλαβέσθαι, οὕτως οὐδὲ τῶν βιωτικῶν πραγμάτων· ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν τῇ τελευτῇ καταλύεται, τὰ δὲ καὶ πρὸ τῆς τελευτῆς χειμάῤῥου παντὸς ὀξυῤῥεπέστερον παραῤῥεῖ. Τὰ δὲ μέλλοντα οὐ τοιαῦτα· οὐκ οἶδε γὰρ μεταβολὴν, οὐ δέχεται τροπὴν, οὐκ ἐπίσταται γῆρας, οὐκ ἔχει τινὰ ἀλλοίωσιν, ἀλλ' ἀκμάζει διηνεκῶς. καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς αὐτῆς εὐπρεπείας μένει. Ὥστε εἰ δεῖ ἀφανῆ καὶ ἄδηλα εἰπεῖν καὶ ἄπιστα, τὰ παρόντα δεῖ λέγειν πράγματα, καὶ μὴ παραμένοντα τοῖς κεκτημένοις, ἀλλ' ἀμείβοντα τοὺς δεσπότας, καὶ καθ' ἑκάστην ἡμέραν ἀπὸ τούτου πρὸς ἕτερον μεταπηδῶντα, καὶ πάλιν ἀπ' ἐκείνου πρὸς ἄλλον.
thought_title: The certainty of future goods versus the uncertainty of present ones
orientation: Chrysostom is addressing his congregation, contrasting how people trust unseen outcomes in farming and trade with their hesitation to trust God's promised rewards.
pass_a_gloss: How then is it absurd, in the case of the affairs of life, to look at the unseen things before the visible things, and to endure the labors before the wages, and first bearing all the difficult things, then to await the good things that come from them, and being urged on by hopes of unseen things, so to lay hold of the visible things; but in the case of God to hesitate and to doubt, and to demand the rewards before the labors, and to appear more fainthearted than farmers and sailors? For not only in this respect will we appear worse than they, being vexed at what is to come, but also in another respect not less than this. What then is this? That those men, not even being able to be confident about the end at all, do not even so withdraw from their labors; but you, having a trustworthy guarantor of the crowns, do not even so imitate their endurance. For the farmer often, after casting the seeds, and tending the earth, and seeing the crops flourishing, either hail, or blight, or locust, or some other such blow having come upon them, fell away from the reward of his labors, and after his many sweats returns home with empty hands. And the merchant again, after running across a great sea, bringing his ship laden, often at the very mouth of the harbor, winds having fallen upon him, having dashed against some rock, barely escaped, having saved his body naked. And in all the affairs of life simply, many such misfortunes often happen near the end, as is likely. But in the case of your contests this is not so; but it is necessary by all means that the one who has contended, the one who has sown piety, and has borne many labors, attain the end. For God did not entrust the rewards of these labors to irregularities of weather, nor to currents of winds; but they are stored up in the heavens, in the inviolable treasuries. For this reason Paul also said: Affliction works endurance, and endurance works provenness, and provenness works hope, and hope does not put to shame. Do not then say that the things to come are unseen; for if you should wish to examine with precision, they are far more visible than the things in hand. And this very thing again Paul showing to us, calls the one things eternal, and the other things temporary, by the temporary making clear their corruptibility. For before it appears it flies away, and it runs off before it arrives, and their changes are swift, and their possession is untrustworthy. This one might see happening in the case of wealth and glory and power, and in the case of the beauty of bodies, this also in the case of strength and of all the other affairs of life simply. For this reason also the prophet, mocking those who live in luxury and rage over money and all the rest of the show, says: As things standing, they reckoned these things, and not as things fleeing. For just as it is not possible to lay hold of a shadow, so neither of the affairs of life; but some are dissolved by death, and others even before death flow away more swiftly than any winter torrent. But the things to come are not such; for they know no change, they admit no turning, they do not know old age, they have no alteration, but they flourish perpetually, and remain in the same beauty. So that if one must call things unseen and unclear and untrustworthy, one must call the present affairs, which do not remain with those who possess them, but change their masters, and each day leap from this one to another, and again from that one to another.

choices.why: keeps the visual metaphor of things not visible to bodily eyes, matching the contrast with φανερῶν (visible) throughout the section
captures the smallness of soul implied by the compound, fitting the moral contrast with farmers and sailors
renders the legal-commercial force of the term, which fits the section's imagery of wages and rewards
preserves the sense of tested and approved character, distinct from mere testing
keeps the legal-religious sense of asylum, that no one can plunder these treasuries
renders the comic, satirical force of the verb, which fits the prophet's ridicule of the rich

pass_b_english: How then is it not absurd that in the affairs of this life we look at what is unseen before what is visible, and endure labors before the wages, and first bear all the hardships and only then expect the good that comes from them, and are stirred by hopes of unseen things to take hold of visible things in this way—yet when it comes to God we hesitate and doubt, and demand the rewards before the labors, and show ourselves more fainthearted than farmers and sailors? For we will appear worse than them not only in this respect, by being impatient about the future, but also in another respect no less than this. What is that? They, even when they cannot be entirely confident about the outcome, still do not abandon their labors; but you, though you have a trustworthy guarantor of the crowns, still do not imitate their endurance. The farmer, after casting the seed and tending the ground and seeing the crops flourishing, often loses the reward of his labors when hail or blight or locusts or some other such blow falls on them, and after his many sweats returns home with empty hands. And the merchant again, after crossing a great expanse of sea with his cargo ship fully loaded, often strikes a rock just at the mouth of the harbor when winds rush in, and barely escapes with his life, naked. And in all the affairs of this life, many such disasters often happen right at the end. But in your contests this is not so. The one who has contended, who has sown godliness and borne many labors, must by all means attain the end. For God has not entrusted the rewards of these labors to the unevenness of the air or the force of the winds, but they are stored up in the heavens, in inviolable treasuries. This is why Paul also said, "Affliction produces endurance, and endurance produces provenness, and provenness produces hope, and hope does not put us to shame" (Romans 5:3-5). So do not say that the things to come are unseen. For if you are willing to examine carefully, they are far more visible than the things in hand. And Paul, showing us this very thing again, calls the one things eternal and the other things temporary, revealing their corruptibility by the word "temporary." For before it appears it flies away, and it runs off before it arrives, and its changes are swift, and its possession is untrustworthy. One may see this happening with wealth and glory and power, and with beauty of body, and with strength and with all the other affairs of this life. This is why the prophet, mocking those who live in luxury and rage after money and all the rest of the illusion, says, "They considered these things as standing, and not as fleeing." For just as it is impossible to grasp a shadow, so it is with the affairs of this life. Some are dissolved by death, and others flow away even before death, more swiftly than any winter torrent. But the things to come are not like this. They know no change, they admit no turning, they do not understand old age, they have no alteration, but they flourish continually and remain in the same beauty. So if one must call anything unseen and uncertain and untrustworthy, it is the present things that should be called so—things that do not remain with those who possess them, but change masters and leap every day from this person to another, and again from that one to another.
